mainTopic: What the words אִישׁ and כִּי יַפְלִיא in the פסוקים of ערכין and נזיר come to teach: גוים, a מופלא סמוך לאיש, and finally a Torah hint for הֶיתֵּר נְדָרִים.
overview: The גמרא rejects a proposal about what the פסוק of נזיר excludes for גוים, because רבי יוחנן says that rule is a הלכה למשה מסיני. It then asks why ערכין needs the word אִישׁ to include גוים, since a היקש to נדרים and a ברייתא on אִישׁ אִישׁ already include them. The answer is that אִישׁ includes a מופלא סמוך לאיש, and according to the view that this law is only דרבנן, it includes a near-adult גוי. That answer fits only one view about whether גוים can be valued or can make the vow. For the other view, רב אדא בר אהבה says כִּי יַפְלִיא teaches that an adult גוי who cannot clearly express a vow cannot make one. Next the גמרא asks why כִּי יַפְלִיא is written in נזיר. It tries ידים שאינן מוכיחות, which fits only אביי, and then רבי טרפון's rule, which the רבנן reject. Finally it says the phrase is needed for רבי אליעזר, who learns הֶיתֵּר נְדָרִים from the doubled כִּי יַפְלִא: one for forbidding and one for releasing.

steps.title: End of the proposal: גוים can still be נזירים
steps.stepSummary: The proposal finishes: without a source we might think גוים cannot be נזירים at all, so the word אִישׁ teaches that they can.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think they cannot be נזירים at all, so the פסוק says 'man' to include them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it began before this section: the exclusion of גוים applies only to one specific rule, while the word אִישׁ shows that גוים can still become נזירים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proposal splits the law in two. The word אִישׁ includes גוים in נזירות itself, and the exclusion of גוים applies only to a narrower rule. That narrower rule is that a son may use his father's money set aside for נזיר offerings.

keyTerms.meaning: One might have thought
The פסוק teaches (by saying)
נזירים, people who took a vow of נזירות
Man; read here as a word that includes more people

phrases.english: One might think that they would not be nazirites at all —
phrases.notes: 'They' means the גוים, who were being discussed just before this.

phrases.english: therefore the verse says: 'Man'!

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל לֹא יְהוּ נְזִירִין תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר אִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a proposed answer that began before this section.

steps.title: Rejected: that rule is a הלכה למשה מסיני
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן said the father's-money rule is a הלכה למשה מסיני, so a פסוק cannot be what limits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't רבי יוחנן say that this rule about a נזיר is a הלכה given to משה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proposal from step 1 by quoting רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that a son may use his father's money for נזיר offerings is not written in the תורה. It is a הלכה למשה מסיני. A פסוק cannot come to exclude גוים from a rule that the פסוק never taught in the first place.

keyTerms.meaning: But wasn't it stated? (introduces a known teaching)
Here: a הלכה למשה מסיני, a law passed down orally from משה
Regarding a נזיר

phrases.english: But wasn't it stated that Rabbi Yochanan said:
It is a halacha (passed down from Moshe) regarding a nazir.
phrases.notes: He's talking about the rule that a son may use his father's leftover נזיר money for his own offerings.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאִיתְּמַר אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֲלָכָה הִיא בְּנָזִיר
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proposal that the פסוק excludes גוים only from the father's-money rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That rule comes from a הלכה למשה מסיני, not from a פסוק, so a פסוק cannot limit it.

steps.title: Why does ערכין need the word אִישׁ?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק of ערכין needs אִישׁ to include גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do I need 'When a man shall clearly utter a vow according to your valuation' in ערכין?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge: the word אִישׁ in the פרשה of ערכין seems to be unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption being tested is that אִישׁ in ערכין comes to include גוים. The גמרא is about to show that this inclusion is already known from somewhere else, which would leave the word with nothing to teach.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
ערכין: vows to donate the fixed 'value' of a person to the Temple
Why do I need it?
Clearly utter (express a vow)

phrases.english: If so
'When a man shall clearly utter a vow according to your valuation,'
stated about valuations, why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי אִישׁ כִּי יַפְלִא נֶדֶר בְּעֶרְכְּךָ בַּעֲרָכִין לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to another use of the word אִישׁ, this time in ערכין.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that אִישׁ in ערכין comes to include גוים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A word in the תורה should teach something new; if גוים are already included some other way, this word looks extra.

steps.title: גוים are already included through the comparison to נדרים
steps.stepSummary: ערכין are compared to נדרים, and a ברייתא learns from אִישׁ אִישׁ that גוים can make נדרים, so גוים are already included in ערכין.
steps.simpleTranslation: ערכין are compared to נדרים by the פסוק 'a man shall clearly utter a vow according to your valuation'. A ברייתא on נדרים says the double 'man, man' includes גוים, who can vow offerings like a Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its question from step 3 by showing exactly where we already learn that גוים are included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof works in two links. The פסוק of ערכין uses the word נֶדֶר, which creates a היקש linking ערכין to נדרים. The ברייתא learns from the double אִישׁ אִישׁ that גוים can make נדרים and נדבות, so through the היקש גוים are automatically included in ערכין too.

keyTerms.meaning: After all; since we already know
Is compared (by a היקש, a link drawn between two topics in the פסוק)
To include
Voluntary gift offerings

phrases.english: After all, aren't valuations compared to vows,
as the verse says:
'When a man shall clearly utter a vow according to your valuation,'
And wasn't it taught regarding vows: 'Man'?
What does the verse teach by saying 'man, man'?
To include the gentiles,
that they can vow vow-offerings and gift-offerings like a Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the evidence behind the question in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: That גוים are already included in ערכין without the word אִישׁ.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The היקש of ערכין to נדרים, together with the ברייתא on אִישׁ אִישׁ in ויקרא 22:18.

steps.title: אִישׁ in ערכין includes a child about to become an adult
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats the question, then answers that אִישׁ in ערכין comes to include a מופלא סמוך לאיש.
steps.simpleTranslation: So why do I need 'when a man shall clearly utter' in ערכין? Rather, this 'man' is needed to include a child in the year before adulthood who understands vows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats its question one more time and then gives a new job to the word אִישׁ in ערכין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since גוים are already covered by the היקש, the word אִישׁ must teach something else. It includes a מופלא סמוך לאיש: a child in the year before adulthood who shows he understands what a vow means. His vow of ערכין counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather
It is needed for
To include
A child close to adulthood (the year before) who understands vows

steps.confusionAlert: Here אִישׁ does NOT come to include גוים, because that was already covered in step 4. It now includes a near-adult child.

phrases.english: So why do I need 'when a man shall clearly utter' in valuations?
Rather, this word 'man'
is needed to include
a child near adulthood who understands vows.
phrases.notes: Literally 'one who is clear, close to being a man': in the year before בר מצוה or בת מצוה, he shows he understands what he vowed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הַאי אִישׁ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְאֵיתוֹיֵי מוּפְלָא סָמוּךְ לְאִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of steps 3 and 4 by giving אִישׁ a different job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the extra word to teach a different law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אִישׁ in ערכין looked like it came to include גוים, which made it unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: אִישׁ includes a מופלא סמוך לאיש in ערכין.

steps.title: What about the view that a near-adult's vow is only דרבנן?
steps.stepSummary: The answer in step 5 fits the view that a near-adult's vow counts מדאורייתא, but not the view that it counts only מדרבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says a near-adult's vow counts by תורה law. But for the one who says it counts only by rabbinic law, why do I need 'when a man shall clearly utter'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges its own answer from step 5, because there is a מחלוקת about how strong a near-adult's vow is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a near-adult's vow binds only מדרבנן, a פסוק cannot be its source. That would leave the word אִישׁ in ערכין unexplained again.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well according to the one who says
From the תורה
From the רבנן (a rabbinic law)

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says
that a near-adult's vow counts by Torah law.
But according to the one who says it is rabbinic,
why do I need 'when a man shall clearly utter'?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר מוּפְלָא סָמוּךְ לְאִישׁ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 5 based on a disagreement over whether the near-adult's vow is מדאורייתא or מדרבנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that אִישׁ includes a מופלא סמוך לאיש.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rabbinic law cannot come from a פסוק, so the word is unexplained again according to that view.

steps.title: It includes a near-adult גוי
steps.stepSummary: According to the דרבנן view, אִישׁ teaches that a near-adult גוי can make an ערכין vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include a near-adult child who is a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge in step 6 by saying the פסוק is about a near-adult גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if a Jewish near-adult's vow counts only מדרבנן, the פסוק teaches that a near-adult גוי's vow of ערכין counts מדאורייתא. This gives the word אִישׁ a real job according to both views.

keyTerms.meaning: Of a גוי (who is a גוי)

steps.whatToRemember: The word אִישׁ in ערכין does not come to include גוים in general, because the היקש to נדרים already does that. It includes a מופלא סמוך לאיש. According to the view that this law is דרבנן, it specifically includes a near-adult גוי, מדאורייתא.

phrases.english: To include a near-adult child who is a gentile.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case the פסוק is talking about.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: According to the דרבנן view, the word אִישׁ seemed to have no purpose.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that a near-adult גוי's ערכין vow counts מדאורייתא.

steps.title: The answer works for the view that gentiles can make valuation vows
steps.stepSummary: According to the view that גוים cannot be valued but can make a valuation vow, the explanation from step 7 works well.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says that Jews can be valued but gentiles cannot be valued. One might have thought gentiles cannot make a valuation vow at all, so the verse says "man." According to this view, it is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge. First it shows the one view where the answer from step 7 fits well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two views about גוים and ערכין. In the first view, a גוי can make an ערכין vow but cannot be valued. Under this view, אִישׁ כִּי יַפְלִיא is talking about the one making the vow, so it fits to say it includes a near-adult גוי who understands vows.

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well (opens the first half of a challenge)
Can be valued, meaning someone can pledge their ערך
Can make a valuation vow, pledging someone else's ערך
Fine, it works

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the two words apart. נֶעֱרָךְ is the person whose value is pledged. מַעֲרִיךְ is the person who makes the vow.

phrases.english: This works well for the one who says
the children of Israel can be valued
but gentiles cannot be valued.
One might think they cannot make a valuation vow either,
so the verse says: "Man"
— according to this view, it is fine.
phrases.notes: He means the answer from the last step, that a near-adult גוי can make an ערכין vow, fits here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the answer from step 7 against the first of two views and finds that it fits.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer of step 7, that אִישׁ includes a near-adult גוי making an ערכין vow
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is the first half of a הניחא-אלא challenge. It shows where the answer works so that the next step can show where it fails.

steps.title: The answer fails for the view that gentiles can be valued
steps.stepSummary: According to the view that גוים can be valued but cannot make the vow, the word אִישׁ is about the person being valued. Age does not matter for that person, so why does the Torah say כִּי יַפְלִיא?
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to the one who says Jews can make a valuation vow and gentiles cannot, one might have thought gentiles also cannot be valued, so the verse says "man." Even a month-old baby can be valued. So why do I need "when he shall clearly utter"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the second view and shows that the answer from step 7 does not work there. The words כִּי יַפְלִיא seem to have no purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this view, אִישׁ teaches that a גוי can be valued. The one being valued does not need to understand anything, since even a month-old baby has a value. So כִּי יַפְלִיא, which is about understanding vows, cannot be about a near-adult גוי being valued, and its purpose is unclear again.

keyTerms.meaning: A month-old baby, the youngest age that has a fixed ערך
Someone who can be valued
"When he shall clearly utter" (a vow)

phrases.english: But according to the one who says:
the children of Israel can make a valuation vow,
but gentiles cannot make a valuation vow.
One might think they cannot be valued either,
so the verse says: "Man" —
even a month-old baby
can be valued,
so why do I need "when he shall clearly utter"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the הניחא-אלא challenge begun in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of כִּי יַפְלִיא according to the view that גוים can be valued but cannot make the vow
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In this view אִישׁ refers to the one being valued, and that person needs no understanding. So the phrase about clearly uttering a vow has nothing left to teach.

steps.title: It teaches about an adult gentile who cannot express a vow
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה says כִּי יַפְלִיא teaches about an adult גוי who cannot clearly express a vow. His vow does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: It comes to include an adult gentile who, even though he is an adult, does not know how to clearly utter a vow.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה answers the question from step 9 by finding a new lesson in כִּי יַפְלִיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being an adult is not enough for a גוי's vow to count. He must also be able to express the vow clearly. כִּי יַפְלִיא teaches this, so it is not extra.

keyTerms.meaning: To include, meaning to teach a new case
To clearly express a vow

steps.whatToRemember: For a גוי, being an adult is not enough. His vow counts only if he can clearly express it, and this is the lesson of כִּי יַפְלִיא.

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
It comes to include an adult gentile,
who, even though he is an adult —
does not know how to clearly utter a vow.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the extra words a new lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under the second view, כִּי יַפְלִיא seemed to have nothing to teach.
steps.terutzMaskana: כִּי יַפְלִיא teaches that an adult גוי who cannot clearly express a vow cannot make one.

steps.title: Why does the Torah say "clearly utter" for נזירות?
steps.stepSummary: נזירות is already compared to נדרים, so why does the Torah need to write כִּי יַפְלִיא in the פרשה of נזיר?
steps.simpleTranslation: But "when he shall clearly utter," which the Merciful One wrote about naziriteship, why do I need it? After all, naziriteship is compared to vows, so why do I need "when he shall clearly utter"?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that ערכין is settled, the גמרא asks the same kind of question about the words כִּי יַפְלִיא in the פרשה of נזיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah compares נזירות to נדרים, so any rules about who can make a vow should already carry over to נזירות. That makes the words כִּי יַפְלִיא in the נזיר verse look extra, and the גמרא asks what they teach.

keyTerms.meaning: The vow of becoming a נזיר
After all, since
Was compared (by a היקש) to
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: But: "When he shall clearly utter"
which the Merciful One wrote about naziriteship,
why do I need it?
After all, naziriteship is compared to vows,
so why do I need "when he shall clearly utter"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: ״כִּי יַפְלִיא״ דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא גַּבֵּי נְזִירוּת, לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining כִּי יַפְלִיא in ערכין, the גמרא asks the same question about the same words in נזירות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The words כִּי יַפְלִיא in the פרשה of נזיר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: נזירות is compared to נדרים, so the rules of vows already apply to it. The phrase therefore looks unnecessary.

steps.title: The extra words include unclear partial vows
steps.stepSummary: כִּי יַפְלִיא in the פרשה of נזיר comes to include ידים שאינן מוכיחות. The גמרא notes that אביי and רבא argue about whether such unclear partial vows count.
steps.simpleTranslation: The extra words come to include unclear partial vow-statements. אביי and רבא argue about this: אביי says they count as a vow, and רבא says they do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 11. It says כִּי יַפְלִיא is needed to include a vow said in unclear, partial wording, and it quotes a מחלוקת about that very case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ידים are partial statements that hint at a vow without saying it fully. When they are 'not clear', you cannot be sure what the person meant. The answer says the extra כִּי יַפְלִיא teaches that even such unclear hints make a vow. But the גמרא right away shows that אביי and רבא disagree about this, which sets up the next challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: To include (to bring in an extra case)
"Handles": partial words that point to a vow
That do not clearly show what is meant

phrases.english: To include ambiguous intimations.
phrases.notes: Think of a person who says only part of a vow formula, so it's not clear he really meant a vow.

phrases.english: As it was stated:
Regarding ambiguous intimations,
Abaye said: they are valid intimations.
Rava said: they are not valid intimations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11 by giving the extra כִּי יַפְלִיא its own job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns a new teaching to the extra words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כִּי יַפְלִיא in נזיר looks unneeded, because נזירות is already compared to נדרים.
steps.terutzMaskana: It comes to include unclear partial vow-statements (ידים שאינן מוכיחות).

steps.title: This answer fails according to רבא
steps.stepSummary: The first answer fits אביי. But רבא says unclear partial vows do not count, so for him the extra words still need a reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: For אביי this works. But according to רבא, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 12. רבא holds that unclear partial vows do not count, so for him the words cannot be teaching that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An answer has to work for everyone. For רבא, ידים שאינן מוכיחות are not a vow at all. So he cannot use כִּי יַפְלִיא to include them, and the question from step 11 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: It works out well
What is there to say? (the answer does not fit this view)

phrases.english: According to Abaye, it works well.
But according to Rava,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאַבָּיֵי נִיחָא. אֶלָּא לְרָבָא, מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 12 by showing it only works for one side of the מחלוקת.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that כִּי יַפְלִיא includes ידים שאינן מוכיחות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא holds such unclear partial vows do not count, so for him the words cannot teach this.

steps.title: The words teach רבי טרפון's rule about clear vows
steps.stepSummary: A new answer: כִּי יַפְלִיא is needed for רבי טרפון. He holds that נזירות takes effect only through a clear, definite statement.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, כִּי יַפְלִיא is needed for what רבי טרפון teaches. רבי יהודה said in his name: none of them is a נזיר, because נזירות was given only for a clear statement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the first answer and gives a new one. The extra words are the source for רבי טרפון's rule that a doubtful נזיר vow does not take effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי טרפון reads הַפְלָאָה as a clear, definite statement. So if people take a נזיר vow as part of a bet about something uncertain, none of them becomes a נזיר. The extra כִּי יַפְלִיא is where he learns this.

steps.terutzMaskana: The words teach that נזירות requires a clear, definite statement (רבי טרפון).

steps.title: This answer fails according to the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: The second answer only works for רבי טרפון. The רבנן disagree with him, so for them the extra words still need a reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for רבי טרפון. But according to the רבנן, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second answer the same way it challenged the first. The רבנן do not accept רבי טרפון's rule, so they cannot use the words for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן argue with רבי טרפון about doubtful נזיר vows. Since they do not learn his rule from כִּי יַפְלִיא, the question returns: for them, why is the phrase written?

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well (for one view)
The Sages (the majority view)

steps.title: The words are needed as a source for releasing vows
steps.stepSummary: A final answer: the phrase is needed for the ברייתא about הֶיתֵּר נְדָרִים. The first view there says releasing vows has no clear source in the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the phrase is needed for what is taught in a ברייתא: the release of vows floats in the air and has nothing to lean on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its third answer. The extra words connect to the topic of releasing vows. This step quotes the opening view of the ברייתא and sets up רבי אליעזר's view, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חכם can release a person from his vow. The first view in the ברייתא says this law 'floats in the air', meaning it has no clear source in the Torah. The answer becomes clear only in the next step, where רבי אליעזר finds a source in the double כִּי יַפְלִיא.

keyTerms.meaning: The release of vows by a חכם
Float in the air (no clear Torah source)
Something to lean on (a source in the Torah)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Floats in the air' does not mean the release of vows is not a real הלכה. It is a real and accepted law. The phrase only means the תורה does not clearly spell out a source for it.

phrases.english: Rather: it is needed for what is taught:
The release of vows —
floats in the air,
and has nothing to lean on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer of step 14, which fit only רבי טרפון, with a new use for the words: the Torah hint for הֶיתֵּר נְדָרִים according to רבי אליעזר, which step 17 completes.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New source-assignment for the extra words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The words were thought to teach רבי טרפון's rule, but the רבנן disagree with that rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words serve as the Torah's hint for הֶיתֵּר נְדָרִים, as explained in the next step.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר learns the release of vows from the doubled phrase
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר says releasing vows does have a source. כִּי יַפְלִא is written twice: once to make a vow forbidden and once to release it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: they do have something to lean on. It says "a man, when he shall clearly utter" and "when he shall clearly utter", two times. One statement is for forbidding, and one statement is for releasing.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the ברייתא. It shows why the extra כִּי יַפְלִיא in נזיר is needed: רבי אליעזר uses the doubled phrase as the source for releasing vows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase appears once in the פרשה of ערכין and once in the פרשה of נזיר. רבי אליעזר says one appearance teaches that a vow binds you, and the other teaches that a vow can also be released. That is why the phrase in נזיר is not extra, which fully answers the question of step 11.

keyTerms.meaning: They have something to lean on (a Torah source)
Two times
For forbidding (making the vow binding)
For releasing (undoing the vow)

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא tried three uses for the extra כִּי יַפְלִיא in נזיר. The first fit only אביי, and the second fit only רבי טרפון. The last one stands: the phrase is written twice so that רבי אליעזר can learn from it both that vows bind and that vows can be released.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives הֶיתֵּר נְדָרִים, the release of vows by a חכם, a hint in the Torah. It also explains why the Torah wrote the same phrase in two places.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
they have something to lean on,
as it says: "A man, when he shall clearly utter"
"when he shall clearly utter": two times.
One utterance is for forbidding,
and one utterance is for releasing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא quoted in step 16 and supplies the actual use of the extra words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Releasing vows has a Torah hint: the doubled כִּי יַפְלִיא teaches one statement for forbidding and one for releasing.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The כִּי יַפְלִיא in the פרשה of נזיר is needed for רבי אליעזר's source for הֶיתֵּר נְדָרִים.
